bivy.name: Lunch Counter
bivy.capacity: Large — dozens of parties on summer weekends, spread across a broad bench; scores of pre-built rock windbreaks, though the best-sheltered ones fill first
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and seasonal. Running meltwater usually appears at the upper end of the bench through early and mid summer, but it is not dependable — in a thin snow year or by late season the bench can be dry, so carry a stove and fuel to melt snow.
bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — this camp is above the 7,000 ft threshold that triggers it between May 1 and Sept 30. Bought through recreation.gov, valid for a single climbing trip; carry it and leave a copy in the windshield. Parking at the South Climb trailhead needs a recreation pass, and the climbing pass parking stub satisfies that within Mt. Adams Wilderness in season. Outside that window or below 7,000 ft, a free self-issued wilderness permit is what applies. Human waste must be packed out in the supplied bags.
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the South Climb and effectively the only sheltered ground on the route, a wide rubble bench under Suksdorf Ridge about four miles and 3,700 ft above Cold Springs. Sources put it anywhere from roughly 9,200 to 9,400 ft because the bench is long and people camp at both ends rather than at one spot. The rock walls left by earlier parties are the whole reason to camp here — wind funnels across the bench and an unprotected tent takes a beating — so plan on repairing a wall rather than finding a perfect one. The summit ridge east of here forms the Yakama Nation boundary; the South Climb stays on Forest Service ground, but do not descend or traverse east off the standard line.

bivy.name: Cold Springs / South Climb trailhead
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites plus overflow in the parking area; fills on summer weekends
bivy.water: Unreliable. Treat this as a dry camp and arrive with water. Small springs and Morrison Creek near the road can be running early in the season and gone by late summer.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass is required to park — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass, or a day pass; a valid Mt. Adams Climbing Pass parking stub also works between May 1 and Sept 30. Camping here is below the 7,000 ft climbing-pass threshold, so a free self-issued wilderness permit covers you unless you go above that line. Waste bags are usually stocked at the trailhead.
bivy.notes: Most South Climb parties sleep here the night before, either to acclimatise a little or to get an alpine start without carrying a camp to the Lunch Counter. Facilities are primitive — a vault toilet, no piped water, no developed fee sites. Access is FR 80 to FR 8040 and then FR 8040-500, roughly eight miles of washboarded and rutted gravel with the last three miles steep, narrow and switchbacked; ordinary cars get up it at low speed but a low-slung vehicle can bottom out, and RVs and trailers should not attempt it. The road generally opens around mid-May and is usually clear of snow by the start of July, so early-season parties should expect to park lower and walk.

bivy.name: Morrison Creek Campground
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of primitive sites, several strung along the creek
bivy.water: Morrison Creek runs beside the camp but is seasonal and can be low or dry by late summer; treat what you take and do not count on it in August or September.
bivy.permit: No climbing pass needed at this elevation — it sits well below the 7,000 ft line. A free self-issued wilderness permit covers travel into Mt. Adams Wilderness from here, and a recreation pass applies at the trailheads above.
bivy.notes: The fallback camp when the upper road defeats a vehicle or when Cold Springs is full, about three miles below the South Climb trailhead on the same road. The 2012 Cascade Creek fire burned through here, so shade is patchy and there is standing dead timber to consider when choosing a tent spot in wind. Camping here means driving or walking the last steep section to the trailhead in the morning, which costs about an hour but keeps the option open when the road is rough.

bivy.name: High Camp (Adams Creek Meadows)
bivy.capacity: Moderate — open meadow and bench terrain with many dispersed spots; busy in wildflower season but rarely crowded by alpine standards
bivy.water: Generally reliable through summer. Meltwater streams from the Adams Glacier snout and small tarns feed the meadows, and Killen Creek runs lower on the approach; filter everything, and expect surface streams to shrink late in a dry season.

Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent for trailhead parking. Camp on durable ground and well back from water — this is fragile subalpine meadow.
bivy.notes: The base for the north side, reached by the Killen Creek trail from about 4,600 ft to the PCT and then a boot path up to the meadows below the Adams Glacier. There is no shelter from wind other than what the rock benches give you, and afternoon weather rolls in fast off the north face. Snow lingers here into July in a heavy year, which affects both the boot track and where you can pitch.

bivy.name: Adams Glacier moraine bivy
bivy.capacity: Very small — a few flat gravel or snow platforms for one or two tents; you may have to build a platform
bivy.water: Meltwater from the glacier snout and moraine pools during the day, freezing overnight; workable in warm conditions but not a certainty. Most parties melt snow here rather than depend on running water.
bivy.permit: Cascade Volcano Pass (Mt. Adams Climbing Pass) required — above 7,000 ft, May 1 through Sept 30, single trip, from recreation.gov. Outside that window a free self-issued wilderness permit applies instead. Pack out all human waste.

It is exposed, rockfall from the moraine walls is a real consideration in warm weather, and there is no shelter at all — the trade is a shorter and colder-snow start onto the glacier. Whether the extra carry beats simply starting early from High Camp is argued both ways.

bivy.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge

bivy.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Access is the current problem rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been under a repair closure short of the trailhead, which turns the approach into a long road walk or bike ride — confirm the road status with the ranger district before committing to a weight-carrying plan. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.

bivy.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
bivy.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback
bivy.water: Reliable — the approach streams below the moraine still carry water here later in the season than they do higher up, though the crossings themselves can run high and pushy on warm afternoons
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
bivy.notes: The cabin itself is long gone, and the name now marks a cluster of sites around 4,800 to 5,000 ft with Harrison Camp on the moraine above the lower Coleman. These suit a party arriving late, anyone who wants trees around them in bad weather, or a group that would rather climb from lower down than share the Hogsback. The trade-off is an extra thousand feet on summit day. Backcountry toilets have been maintained here in some seasons but not others, so plan to pack waste out.

bivy.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes
bivy.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
bivy.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
bivy.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Camp Muir
bivy.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover
bivy.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar routes, reached by the roughly 4,500 ft slog up the Muir Snowfield from Paradise. The Public Shelter is first-come and cannot be reserved, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan and carry a tent regardless; it has been closed for maintenance in past seasons and its status is worth re-checking each year. Weather is the main hazard to the camp itself, and the snowfield below is notorious for whiteout navigation, so record your descent bearings before you need them. The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench
bivy.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
bivy.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
bivy.notes: About a thousand feet above Camp Muir past Cathedral Gap, this bench shortens summit day meaningfully and is the usual overflow when the Muir quota is full. The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it. Whether it is sound in a given week is conditions-dependent and worth asking the climbing rangers rather than deciding from a guidebook. Sites are dug into snow, so bring a shovel and expect to build your own platform and walls.

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends
bivy.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
bivy.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.capacity: Very limited, realistically two to four small tents; parties have ended up stacking tents in a vertical line on the slope when the site is busy, which is not a safe arrangement
bivy.water: Snow only. There is no water and no shelter, so carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for the overnight, plus the climbing cost recovery fee, which is unavoidable on this route. Registration is in person at a ranger station and climbing rangers will discuss current route conditions at that point, which on Liberty Ridge is worth treating as part of the planning rather than a formality.
bivy.notes: The standard and effectively only bivouac on Liberty Ridge, a notch of snow and rock partway up the ridge on the Carbon Glacier side. It is exposed to rockfall from Thumb Rock itself and from the bands above, and a fatal rockfall struck tents here in 2019, so site selection within the notch and the timing of your arrival matter more than comfort. Warm afternoons that prevent an overnight freeze are the usual trigger, and the park service advises against the route when the freezing level on the mountain is high. The approach from the Carbon River or Mowich side is long and its own seasonal problem, since those roads open on different schedules and can be closed by washouts or fire.

bivy.name: White River Campground
bivy.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
bivy.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.capacity: 179 individual sites across six loops, plus separate group sites
bivy.water: Potable water available at the campground during the operating season
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park entrance applies, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up on summit morning. bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier camp
bivy.capacity: A broad flat plateau on the ridgeline with room for several parties, though the daily permit quota caps how many can legitimately be there
bivy.water: Usually available — running water is often audible and reachable over the rocks near camp — but this is a snowmelt supply that varies with the year and the week. Bring the means to melt snow and treat found water as likely rather than certain.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry (wilderness) permit required — this is a DIFFERENT authority from the Mt Baker side, and a Forest Service pass does not cover it. Reservation and per-person nightly fees apply — these permits are no longer free. The zone carries a small daily party quota.

bivy.name: Shannon Ridge crest camps, below the park boundary
bivy.capacity: A few small sites along the open ridge; adequate but cramped compared to the Sulphide camp above
bivy.water: Poor. There is essentially nothing between the trailhead streams and the Sulphide Glacier itself, and what does exist on the ridge is gone by late June in most years. Carry water up from the bottom.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE the national park boundary — no backcountry permit needed here, which is the entire reason parties use these sites. The trade is administrative rather than scenic, so decide before you drive out whether you would rather chase a walk-up permit at a ranger station. FS Road 1152 and its spur are low elevation and generally open early in the season with no need for high clearance, which makes this the most road-reliable approach to either mountain. Check where the boundary actually falls on your map before pitching a tent, because the ridge does not advertise it clearly.

bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier high camp
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms only, for one or two parties; no established sites
bivy.water: None dependable — melt snow. Anything running at this elevation is a hot-afternoon accident rather than a supply.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, same as the 6,400 ft camp — through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with fees. Confirm that your permit covers camping this high in the zone rather than assuming.

bivy.name: Lake Ann basin
bivy.capacity: Established sites around the lake basin; popular with hikers as well as climbers and busy on summer weekends
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams through most of the season. Treat it.

bivy.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide
bivy.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.

A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.

bivy.notes: The fallback for parties who could not get a North Cascades backcountry permit, and honestly worse than the camp above — lower, drier, and leaving a much longer summit day. The trade is administrative rather than scenic, so decide before you drive out whether you would rather chase a walk-up permit at a ranger station. FS Road 1152 and its spur are low elevation and generally open early in the season with no need for high clearance, which makes this the most road-reliable approach to either mountain. Check where the boundary actually falls on your map before pitching a tent, because the ridge does not advertise it clearly.

bivy.name: Sulphide Glacier high camp
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms only, for one or two parties; no established sites
bivy.water: None dependable — melt snow. Anything running at this elevation is a hot-afternoon accident rather than a supply.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, same as the 6,400 ft camp — through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with fees. Confirm that your permit covers camping this high in the zone rather than assuming.
bivy.notes: Some parties carry above the main plateau to shorten summit day to the pyramid, camping on the glacier around 7,500 ft. It is fully exposed, on snow, and above any water, so it only makes sense for a party comfortable with a glacier bivy and a settled forecast. The gain over the lower camp is modest for most people, which is why the 6,400 ft plateau remains the norm. If weather is uncertain, the lower camp is the better place to be.

bivy.name: Lake Ann basin
bivy.capacity: Established sites around the lake basin; popular with hikers as well as climbers and busy on summer weekends
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams through most of the season. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness — the lake sits roughly a mile outside the national park boundary, so no park permit is needed to camp here. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required at the Lake Ann trailhead, camping must be at least two miles from the trailhead between mid-May and mid-November, and the standard 12-person wilderness party limit applies. The permit boundary is signed beyond the lake, and every camp past it needs a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit.
bivy.notes: The usual first night for both the Fisher Chimneys and the North Face, and the jurisdictional line running just past it is the single most useful thing to understand about camping on this side of Shuksan — one night at the lake is a Forest Service matter, the next night up on the route is a national park one. The trailhead sits near 4,700 ft and the trail drops before climbing back to the basin, so the return is uphill at the end of a long day. Access is entirely gated by SR 542, plowed to Artist Point on a seasonal schedule and closed with the first serious snowfall in autumn. Snow can linger in the basin into August in a heavy year.

bivy.name: Fisher Chimneys camps, White Salmon and above Winnie's Slide
bivy.capacity: Small platforms for one or two parties at each of two levels — around 6,800 ft where the chimneys top out near the White Salmon, and higher near 7,300 ft above Winnie's Slide
bivy.water: Snowmelt only in practice. Runoff sometimes appears on the rock below the glaciers in warm conditions, but neither site should be planned around finding liquid water.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — these camps are inside the park, past the signed boundary above Lake Ann. Reserve through Recreation.gov or take a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center within 24 hours; fees apply and the zone carries a small daily party quota. A Northwest Forest Pass covers only the parking at the Lake Ann trailhead.
bivy.notes: Camping above the chimneys is what makes Fisher Chimneys a comfortable two- or three-day climb rather than a very long push, and it puts the party above the loose, route-finding-heavy section for summit day. The lower site near the top of the White Salmon is the more common choice and the more scenic; the higher one above Winnie's Slide costs you a steep snow or ice pitch with a full pack. Which is preferable depends on the party and on conditions in the chimneys, and reasonable people disagree. Both are small and exposed, so a party arriving to find them occupied needs a plan.

bivy.name: North Face bivy, where the rib meets the face
bivy.capacity: One party; rough ground with a couple of usable spots, not a camp
bivy.water: Seasonal melt only. Late in the year expect nothing and carry or melt.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the approach leaves Forest Service ground shortly past Lake Ann and the bivy is inside the park. Through Recreation.gov or as a walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; fees apply and the zone quota is small. Do not assume the Lake Ann trailhead pass covers this.
bivy.notes: North Face parties share the early approach with the White Salmon Glacier route through a brushy section before the two diverge, and the usual bivy sits near 5,500 ft where the rib abuts the face, above Price Lake. It is a working bivy chosen for position on a serious route rather than for comfort, and the point of it is an early start onto sustained steep snow and ice. Objective hazard governs everything here: the face is avalanche-prone, particularly early in the season and further left, so timing and a cold night matter more than the site itself. This is a spring-into-early-summer route in most years.

bivy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites
bivy.water: Reliable in summer: the lake and the South Fork Snoqualmie headwater creeks run all season. In winter the whole basin is snow-covered and you melt.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
bivy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. Source Lake is where a party would sleep if it wanted a pre-dawn start without the drive, about an hour in on the Snow Lake trail. Ground here is rough and off the maintained tread, so choose rock or snow rather than making a new clearing. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. Separately for Guye Peak: the old walking approach through the Alpental Community Club's private roads has been closed to climbers, so plan the talus approach from public ground.

bivy.name: Snow Lake designated campsites
bivy.capacity: Multiple designated sites around the lake; heavily used and often full on summer weekends
bivy.water: The lake is reliable water through summer; treat it. Under snow in winter.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead in season. Camping is restricted to designated sites within half a mile of the lake, group size is capped at 12, and campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft in the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — so stoves only. Same trailhead parking rules as Source Lake.
bivy.notes: The busiest destination in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, and a lake basin rather than a climbers' camp, so expect company. It sits north of the divide from the Alpental valley, which means using it as a base for Chair Peak involves crossing the 4,400 ft saddle and dropping to the lake, then reversing that in the morning. For The Tooth and Guye Peak it is the wrong side of the ridge entirely. Its real value to a climbing party is as a legal, established place to sleep when the weather turns or a descent runs late.

bivy.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
bivy.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
bivy.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
bivy.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.

bivy.name: Denny Creek Campground, I-90 exit 47
bivy.capacity: About 33 sites, most reservable, including electric and double sites plus one group site
bivy.water: Potable water provided during the operating season.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. No elevation is recorded here because a confident figure could not be sourced; it sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.

bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, reserved through recreation.gov up to six months ahead; a small number of first-come sites. No wilderness permit needed, and no trailhead pass required to sleep here. Seasonal — closed outside the summer months, so it is not an option for a winter climb.
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Alpental trailhead, roughly a twenty-minute drive back down I-90 and then three miles up the Denny Creek road. The sensible answer for a party arriving late the night before a Tooth or Chair Peak day, since it needs no wilderness permit and no early-morning decisions. Sites go quickly on summer weekends; book ahead rather than driving up hoping. In winter this option disappears entirely and you are back to sleeping in the valley towns or driving up in the dark.

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42
bivy.capacity: Small forested Forest Service campground, reservable sites
bivy.water: Water availability here varies by year and is not guaranteed — confirm before relying on it and carry enough for the night otherwise.
bivy.permit: Campground fee via recreation.gov; seasonal operation only, closed outside the summer months. No wilderness permit or trailhead pass involved.
bivy.notes: Further down the valley than Denny Creek, about 1.5 miles in on Forest Road 55 from exit 42, and the usual fallback when Denny Creek is booked out. The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. Like every developed site on this stretch of I-90 it is a summer-only option. No elevation is recorded here because a confident figure could not be sourced; it sits well below the pass, low in the South Fork valley.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.

bivy.name: Lake Stuart
bivy.capacity: Several established sites around the lake, but the real limit is the permit quota — the Stuart Zone releases only a small number of group permits per night
bivy.water: The lake and Mountaineer Creek are reliable all season; treat lake water and camp well back from the shore
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area, STUART ZONE, Wenatchee River Ranger District. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through Oct 31, allocated by group through the Recreation.gov advance lottery with a small remainder released otherwise. Outside that window no overnight permit is required, though self-registration at the trailhead is asked for. Day use needs only the free trailhead permit plus a Northwest Forest Pass.
bivy.notes: The north-side staging point, used by parties approaching the Complete North Ridge or the Sherpa Glacier from Mountaineer Creek rather than walking around the peak from Ingalls. Road access is seasonal in a way the Teanaway side is not: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road generally closes from November until sometime in May, which shortens the window from this side considerably. Where the Stuart Zone boundary falls relative to the upper Mountaineer Creek basin and the Stuart Glacier moraine is genuinely unclear — some maps place Stuart's north side outside the permit zones — so a party bivying high in that basin should confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District rather than assume, and carry a permit if in doubt.

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.

bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.

bivy.name: Lake Stuart
bivy.capacity: Several established sites around the lake, but the real limit is the permit quota — the Stuart Zone releases only a small number of group permits per night
bivy.water: The lake and Mountaineer Creek are reliable all season; treat lake water and camp well back from the shore
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area, STUART ZONE, Wenatchee River Ranger District. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through Oct 31, allocated by group through the Recreation.gov advance lottery with a small remainder released otherwise. Outside that window no overnight permit is required, though self-registration at the trailhead is asked for. Day use needs only the free trailhead permit plus a Northwest Forest Pass.
bivy.notes: The north-side staging point, used by parties approaching the Complete North Ridge or the Sherpa Glacier from Mountaineer Creek rather than walking around the peak from Ingalls. Road access is seasonal in a way the Teanaway side is not: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road generally closes from November until sometime in May, which shortens the window from this side considerably. Where the Stuart Zone boundary falls relative to the upper Mountaineer Creek basin and the Stuart Glacier moraine is genuinely unclear — some maps place Stuart's north side outside the permit zones — so a party bivying high in that basin should confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District rather than assume, and carry a permit if in doubt.
